challenges.name: cache-drift-quiz
challenges.title: Who put the old price back?
challenges.description: A Redis MONITOR trace of the price edit that did not show up, and a proposed change to the update path. Read the order of the commands, not the order of the code.

questions.question:
Two API instances share one Redis. A course page request on catalog-api-2 and a price edit on admin-api ran at the same time (Redis MONITOR, merged with the PostgreSQL log):

10:00:00.000 [catalog-api-2] GET course:c1 -> (nil)
10:00:00.002 [catalog-api-2] SELECT * FROM courses WHERE id = 'c1'   -- returns price_vnd 249000, answers at .478
10:00:00.120 [admin-api]     UPDATE courses SET price_vnd = 199000 WHERE id = 'c1'; COMMIT
10:00:00.125 [admin-api]     DEL course:c1 -> (integer) 0
10:00:00.482 [catalog-api-2] SET course:c1 '{"id":"c1","priceVnd":249000,...}' EX 3600 -> OK

Statement: "Redis now serves 249000 for course:c1 because catalog-api-2 read the row before the UPDATE committed and stored it after the DEL; without another invalidation it stays wrong until the key expires."
questions.explanation: True. The DEL did its job at .125: the key was gone (it even returned 0 because nothing was cached). The problem is the request that started earlier. Its SELECT saw the committed row of that moment (249000), and its SET arrived at .482, after both the COMMIT and the DEL, so it re-created the key with the old price and a fresh one-hour TTL. Nothing else touches the key, so every reader gets 249000 until 11:00. The misconception is that "update the database, then delete the key" is enough on its own: it closes the drift from a missing invalidation, but a slow reader can still re-populate the key with a value it loaded before the change. A version check on the fill (or a short delayed second delete) is what closes this window.

False. The admin SET at about .125 writes 199000, but catalog-api-2 still sends its SET at .482 with the row it read at .002, and in Redis the last write wins: course:c1 ends with 249000 again, for an hour. Writing the new value from the update path does not stop a slower writer, and it adds a second race: two edits whose SETs arrive in the opposite order of their COMMITs leave the older price in the cache. Deleting is safer because a missing key can only be filled by a reader, and a fill that checks a version (or is followed by a delayed second delete) cannot win against a newer change. The misconception is that writing the cache yourself makes it "the latest" value; it is only the latest SET.

challenges.name: cache-drift-invalidate
challenges.title: Fix the cache drift after a price edit
challenges.description:
CatalogService serves the course page (getCourse, cached as course:<id>) and the category page (listCategory, cached as courses:category:<category>) from Redis with cache-aside and a one-hour TTL; PostgreSQL is the source of truth. After an admin lowered "Redis Patterns" from 249000 to 199000 VND, both pages kept the old price for about an hour. A later edit was followed by a manual DEL, yet seconds after it the course page showed the old price again: a request that had loaded the row before the edit stored it in Redis after the edit.

Fix the service with this protocol, which the tests check exactly:
- updateCoursePrice(id, priceVnd) writes PostgreSQL first (db.updatePrice). Once the UPDATE has answered, it invalidates course:<id> and courses:category:<category of the course> (the category comes from the returned row). Invalidating a key means INCR "<key>:ver", then DEL <key>. The update path never SETs a cached value.
- A cache fill (a miss in getCourse or listCategory) reads "<key>:ver" before it queries PostgreSQL. After the query answers, it SETs the key with EX CACHE_TTL_SECONDS only if "<key>:ver" has not changed; otherwise it skips the SET. Either way the request returns what it loaded.
- Keep the validation: a priceVnd that is not a whole number >= 0, or an unknown course id, returns false and changes nothing. A valid edit returns true.

Input (one test case, JSON on stdin): { db: Course[], steps }. Each step starts a request as an actor ({ "as": "A", "getCourse": "c1" }, { "as": "B", "listCategory": "redis" }, { "as": "U", "updateCoursePrice": "c1", "priceVnd": 199000 }), resumes one ({ "resume": "A" }) or moves the clock ({ "advance": 600 }, in seconds). A request with "slow": true sends its next PostgreSQL query, but the answer only arrives at its resume step: a slow SELECT returns the rows as they were when it was sent, a slow UPDATE commits when it answers.

Output: one line per step, printed by the runner: what the request returned ("Redis Patterns 199000", "c1 249000, c2 199000", "not found", "ok", "rejected" or "waiting for PostgreSQL") and, for reads, whether it queried PostgreSQL (db) or answered from Redis (cache). The tests replay edits, slow readers that loaded before an edit, slow edits and invalid edits, and check what every later reader sees.
hints: After an edit has answered, which code can still write course:c1 in Redis? List every SET in the service and ask, for each one, how old the value it writes can be.

Look at two places: updateCoursePrice, which today only talks to PostgreSQL, and the private cached() helper that both readers share. The helper is the only place that fills keys, so a check added there protects the course page and the category page at once.

A similar case on different data: a profile cache user:<id> with a fill that takes 300 ms. At t=0 the fill reads user:7:ver ("4") and starts its SELECT; at t=100 a rename commits, then INCR user:7:ver (now "5") and DEL user:7; at t=300 the fill reads user:7:ver again, sees "5" instead of "4", returns the old name to its own caller and does not SET. The next reader misses and loads the new name.

B getCourse c1 -> Redis Patterns 199000 (db)
